To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the naive CD4 T-cell pool expands through proliferation in healthy children, and that in untreated children infected with human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1), the naive CD4 cell pool is eroded through continuous activation.
in healthy children, expansion of the naive CD4 T-cell pool after early childhood is more dependent on proliferation than was previously appreciated.
the thymic output of T cells is low during early childhood and is not affected by HIV infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the immune system and its role in health and disease.
understanding the mechanisms of HIV disease pathogenesis and how these differ in children from adults.
the development of new methods to detect the presence of HIV-1 infection in infants and children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the CD4 T-cell pool is maintained by the expansion of T-cell clones in healthy children, whereas in children with HIV-1 infection, the CD4 T cell pool is maintained by continuous activation of naive CD4 T cells.

in healthy children, the T cell pool is established by a combination of thymic output and T cell expansion through proliferation, whereas in children infected with untreated HIV-1, the T cell expansion is driven by continuous T cell activation and the thymic output is low.

the CD4 T-cell pool of children with untreated HIV infection is established in a similar manner as in HIV-uninfected children, with the exception that the naive CD4 T-cell compartment is more severely affected by HIV infection than the memory CD4 T-cell population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the naive T-cell compartment in healthy children is established through a combination of proliferation and activation of naive T-cell precursors, whereas in untreated HIV-infected children the naive T-cell population is maintained through proliferation of naive T cells.
HIV-1 infection leads to a loss of naive T cells in the blood, and the mechanism for this loss may be different in children than adults.
the thymic contribution to the CD4 T-cell pool of healthy children is limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in healthy children, the naive T-cell compartment is established by proliferation and not by continuous thymic production.
the naive CD4 T-cell pool expands in healthy children through a combination of proliferation and activation.
the thymic output of new T cells is not as important as we previously thought.
